Nu Holdings posts $1.09 billion quarterly profit, shares rise
sum: Nubank parent Nu Holdings reported third-quarter net income of $1.09 billion on Nov. 12, a 31% increase from a year earlier on a currency-neutral basis and in line with analyst estimates, according to Reuters.

Revenue for the July-September period totaled $6.26 billion, up 37% and roughly matching market expectations, according to Reuters. Shares rose about 4% in extended trading after the results, following a 2% gain during the earnings call.

The company now expects a full-year efficiency ratio of 19% to 19.5%, down from an earlier projection of around 20%, Reuters reported. The ratio measures how much a bank must spend to generate revenue. CFO Rob Livingston told Reuters that hiring ran slower than expected. "We are seeing significant benefits from AI helping us with our capacity and productivity, and so we slowed down our hiring," he said.

Nubank's credit portfolio grew 33%, while the 90-day delinquency ratio rose to 7.3% from 6.7%, according to Reuters. Livingston said the uptick was due mostly to seasonal factors and a risk increase from late last year into early this year. "We're not seeing any evidence of broad-based exogenous worsening in our portfolio," he said.

CEO David Velez said on a call with analysts that Nubank will consider mergers or acquisitions as it expands globally but has a "strong preference" for organic growth, according to Reuters. "The bar would have to be extremely high for us to do a full M&A," he said.

Nubank Shares Slide After Lula's Brazil Election Win, but UBS and JPMorgan Lift Price Targets
sum: Nu Holdings (NYSE:NU) has slipped to its weakest level since June, with the Brazilian digital bank's stock closing in on $11.61, roughly 39% below its record high. The decline accelerated after Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defeated Flavio Bolsonaro in Brazil's closely watched presidential election, a result that disappointed investors who had bet on a market-friendly outcome.

The drop has erased a large slice of the company's valuation: Nu's market capitalization has shrunk to about $56 billion from $91 billion at its peak. The pullback was not unique to Nu. Brazil's benchmark Ibovespa Index fell to 167,921, its lowest close since Aug. 21 and about 20% below its October high, while the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (AMEX:EWZ) slid to $32 from an October peak of $44.

The reaction was violent even by emerging-market standards. Trading on Brazil's exchange was halted by an automatic circuit breaker, the real fell about 10% against the dollar to its weakest level since December 2025, and Brazil's Treasury canceled auctions of inflation-linked and fixed-rate bonds that had been scheduled for Oct. 27 and Oct. 29. Analysts framed the move around fiscal policy rather than any single company: Citi cited investor concern about "fiscal policy, state-owned enterprises, and the broader reform agenda," while ING estimated the budget deficit at 7% to 8% of GDP and net debt at about 70% of GDP. For dollar-based investors, the currency move compounds the local share decline, because a weaker real reduces the dollar value of earnings generated in Brazil.

That matters for a lender. The same analysts said Brazilian banks face the risk that interest rates stay higher for longer, delaying the normalization of asset quality. The central bank had cut the Selic benchmark to 13.75% in September, its fifth consecutive reduction, but the election has made the pace of further easing less certain. Nubank's second-quarter results show why the rate path matters: its net interest margin and delinquency trends are the figures most exposed to a prolonged period of high rates.

Selling pressure also followed confirmation that Nu was in talks to acquire Monzo, the British neobank. In an SEC filing, Nubank acknowledged the discussions but said the two sides could not agree on price.

sum: Nobody at Nu Holdings confirmed a word of it, but the stock still lost $6.6 billion in value before the company had to file paperwork with regulators denying the deal was real.

A single unconfirmed report wiped $6.6 billion off Nu Holdings' market capitalization. On September 28, the stock fell 10% to $12.23 a share, and the trigger wasn't an earnings miss or a regulatory fine. Two days earlier, Sky News had reported that Nubank was in early talks to buy Monzo, the British digital bank, in a deal that could value Monzo at £8 billion to £10 billion, or roughly $10.6 billion to $13.3 billion. Bloomberg confirmed it independently.

Nobody at Nubank said a word publicly for days. Then, on October 1, the company did something it says it doesn't normally do: it filed a Form 6-K with the SEC specifically to knock down a rumor. "As a matter of general practice, the company does not comment on specific opportunities," Nubank wrote. But it made an exception "given the extent of recent media speculation." The bottom line of the filing: Nubank is not pursuing a transaction with Monzo.

Shares popped after hours once the filing hit, clawing back part of the prior selloff. But here's the part that should bother anyone holding Nu stock: the company didn't deny that talks happened. It denied that it is "pursuing a transaction" right now. Sky News reported the conversations were in early stages, with banking sources telling the outlet that any eventual deal would likely mix stock and cash. Monzo was also said to be weighing a fresh funding round or a minority stake sale as an alternative to an outright sale, with Advent International named as one of several private equity firms circling a minority position. None of that reads like a story that started from nothing.

A 10% single-day drop on unconfirmed M&A chatter is not a normal reaction. items.t: Discover the possibilities of an active technology ETF
sum: Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to become the most significant productivity enhancer for the global economy since electricity. It is estimated that electricity contributed a 30.6% increase in labor productivity for global gross domestic product over 32 years1 compared with a hypothetical baseline where this technological advancement never happened.2 AI most likely will surpass that.

Historically, productivity-enhancing technologies are often associated with speculative stock market bubbles. Investors must navigate these responsibly by capturing the upside and mitigating the downside. Active management can make a big difference in these situations.

It’s tempting to compare this infrastructure cycle with the telecom bubble of the late 1990s, but there are many meaningful distinctions. Most notably, this current cycle is funded by the most profitable companies in history—the hyperscalers. These companies operate as natural monopolies, and only at their scale has it even been possible to invent, develop, and finance the significant changes driven by AI. The paradox is that while AI was only possible due to the hyperscalers’ enormous power and scale, AI also initiates the very transition that could potentially disrupt the existing businesses of these natural monopolies. This implies that the infrastructure investments are both offensive and defensive and could continue longer than the market expects.

AI remains a transformative force that is reshaping global markets. So far, the majority of economics associated with this infrastructure boom have accrued to the digital semiconductor and hardware industries, though software and digital advertising companies are also seeing stronger revenue growth as AI spending cascades through the technology ecosystem.

The AI investment cycle is fueling both digital and physical investment booms—from semiconductors and software to power infrastructure and data centers. Demand still exceeds supply, supporting elevated returns across the value chain. The focus for investors is to participate responsibly, manage concentration and valuation risk, and stay adaptable as market dynamics evolve and the next phase of AI adoption unfolds.
